why: The metallic rod is isolated from the ground, so no charge can enter or leave it and its total charge stays zero. The nearby positive glass rod attracts the rod's free electrons to the near face, leaving that face negative; the electrons that moved away leave the far face positive, i.e. carrying the SAME sign as the glass rod. Because the rod as a whole is still neutral, that positive charge on the far face must be exactly equal in magnitude to the negative charge on the near face. So the far side carries charge of the same sign as the glass rod and equal in quantity. The "opposite and equal" alternative describes the NEAR face rather than the far one, and the "lesser in quantity" and "more in quantity" alternatives would leave the isolated rod with a net charge, which is impossible when nothing has been added to it or removed from it.

Once the battery is switched on a uniform field exists between the plates, directed from the positive plate towards the negative plate. The force on a charge is \(\vec{F} = q\vec{E}\), and for an electron \(q = -e\) is negative, so the force is opposite to the field: it points from the negative plate towards the positive plate. The electron is therefore attracted to the positive plate. It cannot be drawn to the negative plate, since that plate carries charge of the same sign as the electron and like charges repel; it cannot stay at rest, since the field is non-zero and so is the force on it; and it cannot travel parallel to the plates, since the force lies along the field, which is perpendicular to them.

By Gauss' law the flux through a closed surface is \(\Phi = q_{\text{enc}}/\varepsilon_{0}\), which depends only on the charge enclosed and not at all on the size or the shape of the surface. Both spheres are centred on the same \(+7\ \mu\)C charge, so both enclose the same charge and carry the same flux, and the ratio is one to one. Working it the long way gives the same answer: the field falls off as \(1/r^{2}\) while the area grows as \(r^{2}\), so \(\Phi = E \times 4\pi r^{2}\) comes to \(7.92 \times 10^{5}\) V m at both 2.0 cm and 4.0 cm. Each of the other choices keeps one of those two \(r\)-dependences and drops the other: 1:4 is the ratio of the two areas, 1:2 is the ratio of the radii, and 1:16 is the ratio of \(r^{4}\).

Coulomb's law in free space gives \(F = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\dfrac{q_{1}q_{2}}{r^{2}} = 9 \times 10^{9} \times \dfrac{1.0 \times 1.0}{(1.0)^{2}} = 9 \times 10^{9}\) N. This is precisely the statement the chapter uses in Sec. 10.4.3 to DEFINE the coulomb: one coulomb is the charge which, placed one metre from another charge of the same magnitude in vacuum, experiences a force of \(9.0 \times 10^{9}\) N. Of the other choices, 1.0 N and 10 N are smaller than the true force by about nine orders of magnitude, and \(9 \times 10^{-9}\) N carries the same digits but with the sign of the exponent reversed.

As printed, this question has no correct option, so no key is asserted for it. The electrostatic force obeys \(F \propto 1/r^{2}\), so the distances are in the ratio \(r_{2}/r_{1} = \sqrt{F_{1}/F_{2}} = \sqrt{(80 \times 10^{-3})/(2.0 \times 10^{-3})} = \sqrt{40} = 6.32\), and none of the four choices is 6.32. Tested the other way round, a doubled distance would leave a force of \(2.0 \times 10^{-2}\) N, four times the distance would leave \(5.0 \times 10^{-3}\) N, half the distance would leave \(0.32\) N and a quarter of it \(1.28\) N, none of which is the printed \(2.0 \times 10^{-3}\) N. Two different single-character repairs each rescue the question but lead to DIFFERENT answers: reading the first force as \(8.0 \times 10^{-3}\) N makes the force ratio 4 and the distance double, whereas reading the second force as \(5.0 \times 10^{-3}\) N makes the ratio 16 and the distance four times as great. Nothing on the printed page decides between those two readings.

Two conductors placed in contact behave as one conductor and must settle at a COMMON POTENTIAL. For an isolated sphere \(V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\dfrac{Q}{R}\), so equal potentials require the charge to be proportional to the radius. Sphere B has half the radius of sphere A, so \(R_{A}:R_{B} = 2:1\) and hence \(Q_{A}:Q_{B} = 2:1\); the \(50\ \mu\)C divides as \(33.3\ \mu\)C on A and \(16.7\ \mu\)C on B. Every other split leaves the two spheres at different potentials, which cannot survive once they are joined: a 1:2 split gives \(V_{A} \propto 8.3\) against \(V_{B} \propto 33.3\); a 4:1 split, which is what sharing in proportion to surface area would give, gives 20 against 10; and an equal 1:1 split gives 12.5 against 25.

A uniform field is one whose lines of force are parallel to one another and equally spaced, which is characteristic (8) of the list of properties of lines of force in Sec. 10.6.3. A pair of charged parallel plates produces exactly that in the region between them, and Sec. 10.6.2 uses this very arrangement as the practical way of setting up a known field, with \(E = V/d\). None of the other arrangements does so: a point charge gives a radial field falling off as \(1/r^{2}\), a line charge gives a radial field falling off as \(1/r\), and charge spread around a circular arc or ring likewise gives a field that changes from point to point. In each of those the spacing of the lines of force varies with position, which by the same characteristic means the field is not uniform.

C sits on the perpendicular bisector, that is the equatorial line, of the dipole formed by A and B. Both charges are the same distance from C, so their fields at C are equal in magnitude; the field of the positive charge A points away from A while the field of the negative charge B points towards B. When these are added the components perpendicular to AB cancel exactly and the components along AB reinforce, so the resultant lies along AB, pointing from the positive charge towards the negative one. Computing it explicitly, with A at \((-2.5, 0)\) cm, B at \((2.5, 0)\) cm and C at \((0, 3.0)\) cm, gives a force on C of about \(37.8\) N directed along AB with a component along the bisector of exactly zero. That vanishing component rules out the perpendicular-bisector direction. It also rules out both "towards point A" and "towards point B", because a vector drawn from C parallel to AB aims at neither charge: both of them lie 3.0 cm below C, so the direction of the force makes an angle of about \(50^{\circ}\) with the line CB.
